To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The genome of the sea urchin, Strongylocentotus purpuratus, provides the tools to study the mechanisms of egg activation, a phenomenon that is essential for the initiation of development.
the sea urchin genome encodes a large number of Ca(2+)-related genes and that the egg has a rich complement of Ca(2+)/phosphorylation signaling modules.
the egg is poised for activation and that fertilization is the trigger for egg activation, which in turn is the trigger for the developmental program.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the Ca(2+)-mediated signaling events that control the initiation of the mitotic cell cycles, the developmental program, and the establishment of the Ca(2(+)) signaling repertoire of the zygote.
the mechanisms that regulate the activation of the zygote developmental program.

the molecular mechanisms that regulate Ca(2+) release and the signaling events that follow, and how this knowledge contributes to understanding the activation of the egg and the developmental program.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sea urchins have a lot to teach us, and we have a lot to learn.
much remains unknown about sea urchin Ca(2+) homeostasis and signaling.
the genome has provided a framework and the functional genomic tools for an unprecedented level of understanding of egg activation and Ca(2+) signal transduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the major components of the Ca(2+)-signaling toolkit and have begun to identify and characterize the Ca(2(+))-dependent signaling pathways that are activated at fertilization.

the sea urchin genome is providing a powerful resource for understanding egg activation, and the sea urchins themselves continue to offer an excellent system to study the mechanisms of this fundamental biological event.

we have learned that the genome is a powerful tool for the discovery of new components and new functions for known components in Ca(2+) regulation and that the sea urchin has become a model system for functional genomic and proteomics approaches.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sea urchin genome has revealed the existence of an elaborate and complex Ca(2+) toolkit in the egg.
the genome has provided a framework for a new era of sea urchins as a developmental model.
the sea urchin genome is a rich resource that will continue to be exploited to answer fundamental questions of egg physiology and development.
